Title: On the Minimum Distances of Some Families of BCH Codes
Text:
On the Minimum Distances of Some Families
of BCH Codes
Yaqi Chen, Hao Chen, Cunsheng Ding and Huimin Lao∗
April 28, 2026
Abstract
BCH codes form an important class of cyclic codes, which have applications in
communication and data storage systems.
Although the BCH bound provides a
lower bound on the minimum distance of BCH codes, determining the true minimum
distances of BCH codes is a very challenging problem. In this paper, we settle the
minimum distances of a number of infinite families of narrow-sense BCH codes.
By explicitly constructing the locator polynomials for minimum weight code-
words, we obtain many families of primitive and non-primitive BCH codes with
d = δ, where d is the minimum distance of a q-ary BCH code of length n, designed
distance δ, and offset b, denoted by C(q,n,δ,b). For primitive BCH codes, we obtain
infinite families of BCH codes over F3 and F4 satisfying d = δ, where δ ∈{5, 6, 7, 8}.
Moreover, we construct several infinite families of q-ary BCH codes with d = δ, where
2 ≤δ ≤q −1. For δ = qt + 1, we prove that the BCH code C(q,qm−1,qt+1,1) has d = δ
for all m satisfying m ≡0 (mod pt), where p denotes the characteristic of Fq. In the
paper by Ding et al., IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory 61(5): 2351-2356, it was conjectured
that the minimum distance of C(q,qm−1,qt+1,1) is always equal to its Bose distance dB.
Our result confirms this conjecture for the case m ≡0 (mod pt). For non-primitive
BCH codes, we construct a family of BCH codes C(q, qp−1
λ
,p+1,1) with d = δ = p + 1,
where p is an odd prime, q = pe with p ∤e and λ | q −1.
Index terms: BCH code, Cyclic code, Linear code.

Let C be an [n, k, d]q linear code. We say that C is distance-optimal if no [n, k, ≥d+1]q
linear code exists. If there is an [n, k, d+1]q linear code and there is no [n, k, ≥d+2]q linear
code, then C is said to be almost distance-optimal. Similarly, if there is an [n, k, d + 2]q
linear code, but there is no [n, k, ≥d + 3]q linear code, then C is called a near distance-
optimal code.
Cyclic codes, first introduced by Prange in [18], are a significant class of linear error-
correcting codes due to their structural properties and efficient decoding algorithms. An
[n, k, d]q linear code C is said to be cyclic if (c0, c1, . . . , cn−1) ∈C implies (cn−1, c0, . . . , cn−2) ∈
C. Each vector (c0, c1, . . . , cn−1) ∈Fn
q can be identified with the polynomial
c0 + c1x + · · · + cn−1xn−1 ∈Fq[x]/(xn −1).
With this identification, any cyclic code C ⊆Fn
q is an ideal of the ring Fq[x]/(xn −1).
Note that every cyclic code is a principal ideal in the ring Fq[x]/(xn −1), generated by
a monic polynomial g(x) of the smallest degree, which divides xn −1. This polynomial
g(x) is called the generator polynomial and h(x) = (xn −1)/g(x) is called the parity-check
polynomial of the cyclic code C.
Let n > 1 be an integer such that gcd(n, q) = 1 and let m = ordn(q) denote the smallest
integer satisfying qm ≡1 (mod n). Let α be a primitive element of Fqm, then β = α

BCH (Bose-Chaudhuri-Hocquenghem) codes are subclasses of cyclic codes ([4, 5, 11]).
A cyclic code of length n over Fq is called a BCH code with designed distance δ if its
generator polynomial takes the form
g(x) = lcm(Mb(x), Mb+1(x), . . . , Mb+δ−2(x))
2


for some integers b and 2 ≤δ ≤n, where lcm denotes the least common multiple of
polynomials. Throughout this paper, we denote by C(q,n,δ,b) the BCH code over Fq with
length n, designed distance δ and offset b. When b = 1, the code C(q,n,δ,b) is referred to as
a narrow-sense BCH code. If n = qm −1, C(q,n,δ,b) is called a primitive BCH code.
By definition, the BCH code C(q,n,δ,b) depends on the choice of β and α. However,
the parameters (i.e., the length, the dimension and the minimum distance) of C(q,n,δ,b) are
independent of the choice of the n-th root of unity β. The defining set of C(q,n,δ,b) with
respect to β is defined by
T = {0 ≤i ≤n −1 : g(βi) = 0},
which also depends on the choice of α and β.
1.2
The motivations of this paper
BCH codes have been a hot research topic in the past 70 years due to the following:
• BCH codes are closely related to a number of areas of mathematics such as algebra,
algebraic number theory, algebraic function fields, algebraic geometry, combinatorics,
elementary number theory, finite fields, graph theory and group theory.
• Some BCH codes are widely used in communication and data storage systems.
Although a lot of progress in the study of BCH codes has been made in the past 70 years
[9], the minimum distance of only a small number of families of BCH codes is settled.
Throughout this paper, let i mod n denote the unique integer r with 0 ≤r ≤n −1
such that i −r ≡0 (mod n). If there exist integers b and δ with 2 ≤δ ≤n satisfying
{(i + b) mod n : 0 ≤i ≤δ −2} ⊆T, where T is the defining set of C(q,n,δ,b), then the
minimum distance of C(q,n,δ,b) is at least δ. This is known as the BCH bound [4]. This BCH
bound provides a lower bound on the minimum distance, which could be tight for certain
types of BCH codes and could be faraway from the true minimum distance for some types
of BCH codes. It is known that C(q,n,δ1,b) = C(q,n,δ2,b) may hold for some δ1 and δ2 with
δ1 ̸= δ2. The largest designed distance defining a BCH code is called the Bose distance
dB [12, p. 171]. Thus we have d ≥dB ≥δ, which provides an approximation to the true
minimum distance.
Determining the true minimum distances of BCH codes is a notoriously hard problem.
Below is a list of results on the true minimum distances of some BCH codes.
• The code C(2,2m−1,δ,1) with δ = 2t + 1 has minimum distance d = δ if either

BCH codes C(q,qm−1,qt+1,1) and presented the following conjecture.

• BCH codes are very important in theory and applications.
• The true minimum distance of only a small number of families of BCH codes is

• Conjecture 1.1 is still open in certain cases.

1.3
The contributions of this paper
In this paper, we settle the minimum distances of some families of BCH codes by explicitly
determining the locator polynomial of a minimum weight codeword. Specifically, we prove
that the minimum distances of the following infinite families of BCH codes are equal to
their designed distances.
• The ternary primitive BCH codes C(3,3m−1,δ,1) with δ = 5, 7, 8 and the quaternary
primitive BCH codes C(4,4m−1,δ,1) with δ = 5, 6, 7, see Theorem 4.1 and Theorem 4.2.
• The q-ary primitive BCH codes C(q,qm−1,δ,1) with 2 ≤δ ≤q −1, see Theorem 4.3.
• The q-ary primitive BCH codes C(q,qm−1,δ,1) with δ = qt + 1, see Theorem 4.4. The
study of this family of codes confirms Conjecture 1.1 in the case m ≡0 (mod pt),
where p is the characteristic of Fq.
• The q-ary non-primitive BCH codes C(q,n,δ,1) with δ = p + 1 and length n = qp−1
λ ,
where p is an odd prime, q = pe with p ∤e and λ | q −1, see Theorem 5.1.

1.4
The organisation of this paper
The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 recalls the necessary preliminaries
on cyclotomic cosets and locator polynomials. Section 3 introduces some auxiliary results
including the inverse of the modified Vandermonde matrix. Section 4 presents some families
of primitive BCH codes with d = δ. Section 5 proves that a family of non-primitive BCH
codes has the property that d = δ. Section 6 concludes the paper.

Preliminaries
2.1
Cyclotomic cosets
Let n be a positive integer and Zn = Z/nZ = {0, 1, . . . , n −1} denote the set of residue
classes modulo n. For any i ∈Zn, the q-cyclotomic coset of i modulo n is defined by
Ci = {iqj mod n : 0 ≤j ≤li −1},
where li is the smallest positive integer such that iqli ≡i (mod n). The smallest integer
in Ci is called the coset leader of Ci. The set of all q-cyclotomic cosets modulo n forms a
partition of Zn.
Let m = ordn(q) and let β ∈Fqm be an n-th primitive root of unity. The minimal
polynomial Mi(x) of βi over Fq is irreducible over Fq and is given by
Mi(x) =

For a BCH code
C(q,n,δ,b) = ⟨g(x)⟩⊆Fq[x]/(xn −1),
the generator polynomial g(x) is the product of some of these minimal polynomials Mi(x).
Consequently, the degree of g(x) and the dimension of C(q,n,δ,b) can be determined by the
sizes of the cyclotomic cosets associated with g(x).
The following two lemmas concern the sizes of cyclotomic cosets.
Lemma 2.1 [12] The size of each q-cyclotomic coset Ci modulo n is a divisor of ordn(q).
In particular, |C1| = ordn(q).
Lemma 2.2 [1] Suppose q⌈m/2⌉< n ≤qm −1, where m = ordn(q). Then for all 1 ≤i ≤
nq⌈m/2⌉/(qm −1), |Ci| = m. In addition, every i with i ̸≡0 (mod q) in this range is a
coset leader.
As a direct consequence of Lemma 2.2, the dimension of the BCH code C(q,n,δ,1) can be
obtained when δ is small compared to n. Specifically, we have the following result.
Lemma 2.3 [1] Suppose q⌈m/2⌉< n ≤qm −1, where m = ordn(q). The narrow-sense
BCH code C(q,n,δ,1) with δ in the range 2 ≤δ ≤min{⌊nq⌈m/2⌉/(qm −1)⌋, n} has dimension
k = n −m⌈(δ −1)(1 −1/q)⌉.

Summary and concluding remarks
In this paper, we settled the minimum distances of a number of infinite families of narrow-
sense primitive BCH codes and an infinite family of narrow-sense non-primitive BCH codes.
In addition, we confirmed a conjecture in [8] about the minimum distance of C(q,qm−1,qt+1,1)
under the condition m ≡0 (mod pt), where p denotes the characteristic of Fq. A summary
of the main contributions of this paper was given in Section 1.3.
The minimum distances of these families of BCH codes were determined by using
Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 via the locator polynomial method. It will be good if this method
can be generalized to other classes of BCH codes and be used to resolve the remaining
cases of Conjecture 1.1.
Notice that the locator polynomial method has been used as a tool for finding the true
minimum distance of cyclic codes for many years (see, e.g., [2, 16]). However, it is not easy
to use this method. Even if a BCH code has a conjectured minimum distance d, it could
be very difficult to confirm the conjectured minimum distance with the locator polynomial
method due to the difficulty in finding a codeword of weight d in the BCH code. This
explains why Conjecture 1.1 is still open in certain cases.

Abstract: BCH codes form an important class of cyclic codes, which have applications in communication and data storage systems. Although the BCH bound provides a lower bound on the minimum distance of BCH codes, determining the true minimum distances of BCH codes is a very challenging problem. In this paper, we settle the minimum distances of a number of infinite families of narrow-sense BCH codes. By explicitly constructing the locator polynomials for minimum weight code- words, we obtain many families of primitive and non-primitive BCH codes with d = δ, where d is the minimum distance of a q-ary BCH code of length n, designed distance δ, and offset b, denoted by C(q,n,δ,b). For primitive BCH codes, we obtain infinite families of BCH codes over F3 and F4 satisfying d = δ, where δ ∈{5, 6, 7, 8}. Moreover, we construct several infinite families of q-ary BCH codes with d = δ, where 2 ≤δ ≤q −1. For δ = qt + 1, we prove that the BCH code C(q,qm−1,qt+1,1) has d = δ for all m satisfying m ≡0 (mod pt), where p denotes the characteristic of Fq. In the paper by Ding et al., IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory 61(5): 2351-2356, it was conjectured that the minimum distance of C(q,qm−1,qt+1,1) is always equal to its Bose distance dB. Our result confirms this conjecture for the case m ≡0 (mod pt). For non-primitive BCH codes, we construct a family of BCH codes C(q, qp−1 λ ,p+1,1) with d = δ = p + 1, where p is an odd prime, q = pe with p ∤e and λ | q −1.
